tip: 'À côté de' means next to, and 'de + le' contracts to 'du': 'à côté du supermarché', never 'de le supermarché'.
'L'addition' is the restaurant bill, not a math sum: 'tu as payé l'addition' = did you pay the bill?
70 = 'soixante-dix' (60+10), 80 = 'quatre-vingts' (4×20), 90 = 'quatre-vingt-dix' (4×20+10). French builds these from 60 and 20.
21 and its cousins normally take a bare 'et', no hyphens: 'vingt et un', 'trente et un'. But most compounds just hyphenate: 'vingt-deux', 'trente-trois'.
'Finir' attaches to the next verb with 'de': 'j'ai fini de manger' = I finished eating. Different verbs pick 'à' or 'de' – 'finir' takes 'de'.
The feminine adds a grave accent: masculine 'fier' becomes 'fière', the same spelling shift as 'premier'/'première'.
'Sortir' uses 'être', not 'avoir', in the past: 'il est sorti' = he went out. Never 'il a sorti' for going out.
'Regarder' already means 'look at', so no preposition follows: 'tu as regardé le film' = you watched the film, never 'regardé à'.
'Rester' takes 'être' even though nobody moves: 'nous sommes restés' = we stayed. Staying put still counts as an 'être' verb.
'Attendre' swallows the 'for': 'j'ai attendu le train' = I waited for the train. Adding 'pour' here would be wrong.
After 'quelque chose', French links the adjective with 'de' and keeps it masculine: 'quelque chose de bon' = something good.
You don't 'pass' an exam in French, you succeed at it: 'tu as réussi ton examen' = you passed your exam.
'Écoute' is the informal command ('tu' form) of 'écouter', used on its own to grab attention.
'Le dimanche' with the article means 'on Sundays' as a habit. Drop the 'le' and 'dimanche' is just one specific Sunday.
For '-er' verbs the 'tu' command drops the '-s': you write 'tu regardes' but 'regarde !' when telling someone to look.
'Commencer' links to the next verb with 'à': 'a commencé à lire' = started to read. The 'à' is required before the second verb.
France runs on a 24-hour clock: 'dix-huit heures' (eighteen hours) is 6 PM. Add 12 to any afternoon time to get the everyday form.
'Porter une barbe' = to wear/have a beard. French uses 'porter' (to wear) for facial hair.
Start a sentence with 'peut-être' and the verb usually jumps ahead of the subject: 'devrions-nous'. To skip the flip, say 'peut-être qu'on...' instead.
French literally says 'I raise myself': 'je me lève' = I get up. Drop the 'me' and 'je lève' just means I lift something else.
'À + le' must merge into 'au': you can't say 'à le restaurant', only 'au restaurant'.
In everyday spoken questions the word order stays the same: 'tu as acheté' said with a rising tone = did you buy?
Feminine countries take 'en' for 'in' or 'to': 'en Espagne' = in Spain. No article – it's not 'dans l'Espagne'.
'Une place' is a seat or spot here, not just a 'place': 'deux places pour le concert' = two seats for the concert.
'Commander' here means to order food, not to command: 'nous avons commandé des pizzas' = we ordered pizzas.
'Entrer' needs 'dans' before a place: 'il est entré dans la pièce' = he entered the room.
'Téléphoner' needs 'à' before the person: 'il a téléphoné à son frère' = he called his brother. You phone 'to' someone in French.
France runs on the 24-hour clock: 'vingt heures' is 8 PM, literally 'twenty hours'. 'Vingt et une heures' would be 9 PM.
'Chercher' already contains the 'for': 'il a cherché ses clés' = he looked for his keys. Never add 'pour' after it.
'Déjà' with the past form 'savais' marks a state that was already true: 'tu savais déjà' = you already knew.
